quests.definition: 'Wake up' means to stop sleeping and become conscious. It's different from 'get up,' which means to physically leave the bed — you can wake up and still stay lying down for a few minutes.
quests.exampleSentence: My alarm rang at six, but I didn't wake UP until the second alarm at seven.
quests.example: My alarm rang at six, but I didn't wake UP until the second alarm at seven.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'WAKE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This is a literal physical process: your brain moves from sleep to alertness. There's no hidden or figurative sense here.
quests.nativeTip: This is about becoming conscious after sleep, not getting out of bed yet.

quests.definition: 'Get up' means to rise from a lying or sitting position, most often out of bed. Compare it with 'wake up': you can wake up and still lie there, but getting up means your body actually moves.
quests.exampleSentence: It was a cold morning, so I didn't want to get UP and leave my warm bed.
quests.example: It was a cold morning, so I didn't want to get UP and leave my warm bed.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: your body physically rises. There's no figurative shift in meaning here — the phrase describes the real action of standing up.
quests.nativeTip: Think about the next step after waking up — leaving the bed itself.

quests.definition: 'Put on' means to place a piece of clothing onto your body. It's the opposite of 'take off.' Notice the particle changes the whole meaning: 'put on' (dress) versus 'put down' (place an object) versus 'put away' (store something).
quests.exampleSentence: It's freezing outside, so put ON your coat before you leave the house.
quests.example: It's freezing outside, so put ON your coat before you leave the house.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'PUT' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Mostly literal — you're physically placing clothing on your body — though English also extends 'put on' to things like makeup or perfume, which aren't literally 'clothing.'
quests.nativeTip: This describes covering your body with something you're going to wear.

quests.definition: 'Turn on' means to activate a device or switch so it starts working. The verb 'turn' originally referred to physically rotating an old-style dial or knob, and English kept the phrase even for buttons and touchscreens.
quests.exampleSentence: It's getting dark in here — could you turn ON the lamp by the sofa?
quests.example: It's getting dark in here — could you turn ON the lamp by the sofa?
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'TURN' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Slightly idiomatic: most modern switches don't actually turn or rotate, but the expression survives from when dials and knobs were common.
quests.nativeTip: You want the lamp to start working, not stop.

quests.definition: 'Turn off' is the direct opposite of 'turn on' — it means to deactivate or stop a device from running. Learners often mix up 'turn off' with 'shut down,' which is used more specifically for computers finishing their shutdown process.
quests.exampleSentence: The movie is over, so let's turn OFF the TV and go to bed.
quests.example: The movie is over, so let's turn OFF the TV and go to bed.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'TURN' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Like 'turn on,' this comes from the old idea of rotating a dial, though it's now used for any kind of switch or button.
quests.nativeTip: The opposite action from switching a device on.

quests.definition: 'Sit down' describes the movement of lowering your body onto a chair or seat. It's often used as a polite instruction, as in 'Please sit down,' when inviting someone to take a seat.
quests.exampleSentence: The waiter showed us to our table and asked us to sit DOWN while he brought the menus.
quests.example: The waiter showed us to our table and asked us to sit DOWN while he brought the menus.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'DOWN' combines with the verb 'SIT' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This is fully literal — it describes the physical action of lowering your body. No figurative meaning applies.
quests.nativeTip: This is about moving your body from standing to a seated position.

quests.definition: 'Come in' means to enter a room or building, often used as an invitation when someone knocks on a door. It contrasts with 'go in,' which describes the same action from the speaker's own point of view rather than an invitation to someone else.
quests.exampleSentence: There was a knock at the door, and I called out, 'Come IN, it's open!'
quests.example: There was a knock at the door, and I called out, 'Come IN, it's open!'
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'COME' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: it describes physically entering a space. The word 'come' rather than 'go' shows the action is toward the speaker's location.
quests.nativeTip: Someone is outside a door, and you want to invite them into the room.

quests.definition: 'Go out' means to leave your home for a social or leisure activity, such as dinner, a party, or a walk. It's commonly used when talking about evening plans or weekend activities.
quests.exampleSentence: We've been inside all week, so let's go OUT for dinner tonight.
quests.example: We've been inside all week, so let's go OUT for dinner tonight.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'GO' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal at its core — you physically leave the house — but it also carries a social connotation, implying you're going somewhere to enjoy yourself rather than just running an errand.
quests.nativeTip: This describes leaving home to do something social or fun.

quests.definition: 'Stand up' means to rise to a standing position from sitting or lying down. It's frequently used in classrooms, courtrooms, and ceremonies as an instruction, such as 'Please stand up for the national anthem.'
quests.exampleSentence: When the judge entered the courtroom, everyone had to stand UP.
quests.example: When the judge entered the courtroom, everyone had to stand UP.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'STAND' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This is a literal description of the body moving from a seated to an upright position — no figurative use is intended here.
quests.nativeTip: This is the opposite movement from sitting down.

quests.definition: 'Take off' means to remove something, especially clothing. It's the reverse of 'put on.' The same phrase also means 'to leave the ground' when talking about planes, so context decides which meaning is intended.
quests.exampleSentence: As soon as she walked into the warm house, she took OFF her heavy coat.
quests.example: As soon as she walked into the warm house, she took OFF her heavy coat.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'TAKE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal here: you're physically removing an item of clothing from your body. (Note: with airplanes, 'take off' becomes closer to a fixed idiom meaning 'leave the ground.')
quests.nativeTip: This is what you do with a jacket when you come indoors and feel warm.

quests.definition: 'Try on' means to put on a piece of clothing temporarily to see if it fits or looks good, usually in a shop's fitting room. It's specific to clothes, shoes, and accessories — you wouldn't use it for food, for example.
quests.exampleSentence: Before buying the shoes, she wanted to try ON a couple of sizes to find the right fit.
quests.example: Before buying the shoes, she wanted to try ON a couple of sizes to find the right fit.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'TRY' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: you're physically wearing the item for a short time to test it, without committing to buying it.
quests.nativeTip: In a clothing store, this is what you do before deciding to buy something.

quests.conceptTitle: Phrasal Anatomy: PUT Put it on
quests.definition: 'Put on' is a separable phrasal verb: with a full noun, you can say 'put on your hat' or 'put your hat on,' but with a pronoun like 'it,' the particle must come after the pronoun — 'put it on,' never 'put on it.'
quests.exampleSentence: Here's your scarf — Put it on before you catch a cold.
quests.example: Here's your scarf — Put it on before you catch a cold.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'Put it on' combines with the verb 'PUT' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: This question is about grammar rather than literal versus figurative meaning: the phrase keeps its literal sense of dressing, but the word order changes depending on whether the object is a noun or a pronoun.
quests.nativeTip: 'Put on' is separable, so a pronoun object usually goes between the verb and the particle.
quests.visualAnchor: 🗝️ PUT + Put it on ➔ PUT Put it on

quests.definition: 'Get on' is used for boarding larger vehicles such as buses, trains, planes, and bicycles — anything you can walk onto or sit up in. It contrasts with 'get in,' which is used for smaller vehicles like cars and taxis.
quests.exampleSentence: Hurry up — we need to get ON the train before the doors close!
quests.example: Hurry up — we need to get ON the train before the doors close!
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: it describes physically boarding a vehicle. The choice of 'on' versus 'in' depends on the size and shape of the vehicle, not the action itself.
quests.nativeTip: This is used for boarding vehicles you can stand up and walk around in, like buses or trains.

quests.definition: 'Get off' means to leave or exit a vehicle you 'get on,' such as a bus, train, or bicycle. Remember the pairing: get on/get off for larger vehicles, and get in/get out for cars and taxis.
quests.exampleSentence: This is our stop — we need to get OFF at the next station.
quests.example: This is our stop — we need to get OFF at the next station.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: it describes the physical act of leaving a vehicle you were riding on top of or inside of, in the 'get on' sense.
quests.nativeTip: This is the reverse action of boarding a bus or train.

quests.definition: 'Get in' is used for vehicles you climb into rather than onto, especially cars and taxis. Its opposite is 'get out (of),' as in 'get out of the car.' Mixing up 'get in' and 'get on' is one of the most common learner errors.
quests.exampleSentence: It's raining hard, so just get IN the car and I'll drive you home.
quests.example: It's raining hard, so just get IN the car and I'll drive you home.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: you're physically climbing into an enclosed vehicle. The particle choice reflects vehicle size, not a different meaning.
quests.nativeTip: This is used for smaller vehicles, like cars or taxis, rather than buses or trains.

quests.definition: 'Hold on' means to wait for a short time, often used on the phone while someone checks information or gets someone else. It comes from the literal idea of holding the phone line rather than hanging up.
quests.exampleSentence: 'Hold ON a second,' she said, 'let me check if he's available.'
quests.example: 'Hold ON a second,' she said, 'let me check if he's available.'
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'ON' combines with the verb 'HOLD' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Slightly idiomatic: originally it meant physically holding the phone connection, but now it's used generally to mean 'wait,' even in situations that have nothing to do with phones.
quests.nativeTip: You want someone to wait a moment, often while you check something.

quests.definition: 'Hang up' means to end a phone call. The phrase comes from old telephones, where you literally hung the receiver back on its hook — the expression stuck even though modern phones don't have hooks.
quests.exampleSentence: He was so angry during the call that he hung UP without saying goodbye.
quests.example: He was so angry during the call that he hung UP without saying goodbye.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'HANG' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Idiomatic: almost no one hangs a phone on a hook anymore, but the phrase still means 'end the call,' showing how expressions can outlive the technology that inspired them.
quests.nativeTip: This describes ending a phone call by putting the receiver back in place.

quests.definition: 'Call back' means to return a phone call, usually because you missed it or couldn't talk at the time. It's a common polite phrase in both personal and professional messages, such as voicemails.
quests.exampleSentence: I missed her call this morning, so I'll call her BACK during my lunch break.
quests.example: I missed her call this morning, so I'll call her BACK during my lunch break.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'BACK' combines with the verb 'CALL' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: The 'back' here signals a return action — calling in response to an earlier call — which is a pattern also seen in 'write back' and 'text back.'
quests.nativeTip: This means returning someone's call after they contacted you first.

quests.definition: 'Pick up' means to lift an object using your hands, usually from the ground or a surface. It's one of the most frequent phrasal verbs in everyday English and also extends to meanings like 'pick someone up' in a car.
quests.exampleSentence: She bent down to pick UP the phone she'd dropped on the floor.
quests.example: She bent down to pick UP the phone she'd dropped on the floor.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'PICK' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal here: your hand physically lifts an object. (In other contexts, 'pick up' can be figurative, such as 'pick up a language' meaning to learn it gradually.)
quests.nativeTip: This describes lifting something from a lower surface, like the floor or a table.

quests.definition: 'Put down' means to place an object onto a surface after holding or carrying it. It's the natural opposite of 'pick up' and is often used in instructions, like asking someone to set an item aside.
quests.exampleSentence: Could you put DOWN that heavy box for a second and help me with the door?
quests.example: Could you put DOWN that heavy box for a second and help me with the door?
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'DOWN' combines with the verb 'PUT' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: it describes the physical motion of lowering an object from your hands onto a surface.
quests.nativeTip: This is the opposite of lifting something up — placing it onto a surface.

quests.definition: 'Give back' means to return something you borrowed to its original owner. Unlike 'give up,' which means to quit or stop trying, 'give back' always involves returning an object, favor, or benefit to someone.
quests.exampleSentence: Don't forget to give BACK my umbrella — you borrowed it last week.
quests.example: Don't forget to give BACK my umbrella — you borrowed it last week.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'BACK' combines with the verb 'GIVE' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: an object physically changes hands and returns to its original owner. There's no hidden meaning to work out here.
quests.nativeTip: This means returning something that belongs to someone else.

quests.definition: 'Plug in' means to connect an electrical device to a power outlet using its cord or plug. It's specific to electrical connections — you wouldn't use it for something like a water pipe.
quests.exampleSentence: The laptop battery is almost dead — can you plug IN the charger?
quests.example: The laptop battery is almost dead — can you plug IN the charger?
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'PLUG' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: the plug is physically inserted into the socket. The meaning matches the action exactly, with no figurative extension.
quests.nativeTip: This is about connecting a device to a power source using its cord.

quests.definition: 'Log in' means to access a computer system, website, or app by entering your username and password. It's the digital equivalent of 'entering' a system, and it's always paired with 'log out' for leaving it.
quests.exampleSentence: You'll need to log IN with your email and password before you can see your messages.
quests.example: You'll need to log IN with your email and password before you can see your messages.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'LOG' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Idiomatic in origin: 'log' once referred to a written record (a ship's logbook), so 'logging in' meant recording your entry — a meaning most users no longer think about.
quests.nativeTip: This is what you do to access an account using a username and password.

quests.definition: 'Log out' means to exit a computer system, account, or app safely, ending your active session. It's the direct opposite of 'log in,' and it's important on shared computers to prevent others from accessing your account.
quests.exampleSentence: Always remember to log OUT of your account when you're using a public computer.
quests.example: Always remember to log OUT of your account when you're using a public computer.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OUT' combines with the verb 'LOG' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Idiomatic, like 'log in' — it no longer refers to an actual written log, but the pairing 'log in / log out' has become a fixed digital-age expression.
quests.nativeTip: This is the action you take when you're finished using an account and want to leave it securely.

quests.definition: 'Clean up' means to tidy a space, removing mess or dirt until it looks organized. It's often used for rooms, kitchens, or after an activity like cooking or a party.
quests.exampleSentence: The kids need to clean UP their room before dinner.
quests.example: The kids need to clean UP their room before dinner.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'CLEAN' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Mostly literal — you're physically removing mess — though the 'up' also suggests completing the job thoroughly, similar to how 'up' adds a sense of finishing in verbs like 'finish up' or 'wrap up.'
quests.nativeTip: This means tidying a messy space so it looks neat again.

quests.definition: 'Throw away' means to discard something you no longer need or want, usually by putting it in the trash. It's commonly used for rubbish, old items, or anything being disposed of.
quests.exampleSentence: This milk has gone bad — you should throw it AWAY.
quests.example: This milk has gone bad — you should throw it AWAY.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'AWAY' combines with the verb 'THROW' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: an object is physically thrown into a bin or discarded, matching the phrase's meaning directly.
quests.nativeTip: This means putting something you no longer want into the trash.

quests.definition: 'Fill in' (used mainly in British English, alongside American 'fill out') means to complete a form or document by writing information in the required spaces. It extends the literal sense of 'filling' empty space with something concrete.
quests.exampleSentence: Please fill IN this form with your name, address, and phone number.
quests.example: Please fill IN this form with your name, address, and phone number.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'IN' combines with the verb 'FILL' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Slightly extended from the literal sense of 'filling' an empty container — here you're filling empty blanks on a form with written information rather than a physical substance.
quests.nativeTip: This is what you do with a form, adding your details into the blank spaces.

quests.definition: This reviews 'get up' from Level 1, but now in the past tense: 'got up.' The particle itself never changes with tense — only the verb 'get' changes to 'got' — which is an important pattern to notice across all phrasal verbs.
quests.exampleSentence: I felt terrible this morning, so I got UP much later than usual.
quests.example: I felt terrible this morning, so I got UP much later than usual.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'UP' combines with the verb 'GET' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal, as before: it still describes physically rising from bed. What's new here is recognizing that the particle stays fixed while the verb form changes with tense.
quests.nativeTip: Think back to the phrasal verb for leaving your bed — now put it in the past.

quests.definition: This revisits 'turn off' from Level 2 in a new context — an oven instead of a light. The meaning doesn't change: you're still deactivating a device. Recognizing the same phrasal verb across different devices helps confirm you've truly learned it, not just memorized one example.
quests.exampleSentence: The cake is done, so please turn OFF the oven before it overheats.
quests.example: The cake is done, so please turn OFF the oven before it overheats.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'OFF' combines with the verb 'TURN' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Idiomatic in origin, like with the lamp example, but now applied to a different device — a good sign that you understand the general rule rather than one fixed sentence.
quests.nativeTip: This is the same phrasal verb from Level 2, now used with a kitchen appliance instead of a lamp.

quests.definition: 'Come back' means to return to a place, especially one connected to the speaker. It pairs naturally with 'go' phrases you've already learned: you 'go out,' and later you 'come back.' Together they describe a full round trip.
quests.exampleSentence: Don't worry, I'll come BACK before it gets dark.
quests.example: Don't worry, I'll come BACK before it gets dark.
quests.particleInsight: The particle 'BACK' combines with the verb 'COME' to specialize or transform its action.
quests.literalVsFigurative: Literal: it describes the physical act of returning to a location. The word 'come' (rather than 'go') shows the movement is toward the speaker's own place.
quests.nativeTip: This describes returning to a place after being away.
